meta.title: Why AI Adoption Stalls at the Engineers | Jonathan Lusk, BirdDog
meta.speakers: Jonathan Lusk (BirdDog); host of The Deal Table
meta.thread_line: 2 threads · engineers are the AI speed bump · AI buys speed, not savings — short clip (~3 min)

snapshot: Short clip (~3 minutes); captured in full.
Host's rule, borrowed from Blockchain.com's Lane Castleman: every employee is **AI first**, but 100% responsible for what ships.
Jonathan Lusk: the adoption bottleneck is engineers, because AI 'completely displaces their identity' — sales people can now build what used to need designers and front-end engineers.
The scarce skill moves to quality control and getting AI-built products into production.
Host: a headline says companies that cut staff for AI now spend more on AI than they saved on labor — the real payoff is speed to market.
Lusk's joke: 'before AI I had three unfinished projects, now I've got 12' — more problems get attempted, which keeps jobs.

themes.title: The AI adoption speed bump is the engineers, not the tools
themes.lead: Lusk says engineers resist AI because it erases their identity, while non-engineers can now build — leaving production and QA as the hard part.
bullets: Sales people — 'very low brow' builders — can now make what used to require **design and front-end engineers**.
The new need: people who quality-control those builds and get them into production, where they behave differently than in the environment they were built in.
Shipping to the public is 'the hardest part right now'; adoption would go much faster if everyone jumped on board.
Lusk sees the lag as BirdDog's advantage; builders on **X** openly share code and step-by-step recipes, making it more accessible.
Host's practice, from Lane Castleman of Blockchain.com: AI first on everything (emails, product, sales), repeated on every weekly team call — with full personal responsibility for the output.
Host: a big conglomerate was surprised a product took BirdDog 30 minutes; bureaucracy blocks large companies from that speed.

quote.text: The speed bump is actually the engineers, you know, that aren't adopting it because it completely displaces their identity as an engineer.

themes.watch: Lusk runs a startup that benefits from incumbents' slow adoption.

themes.title: AI pays back in speed to market, not labor savings
themes.lead: Companies that cut staff to save money are reportedly spending more on AI than they saved — the win is speed and the number of problems you can take on.
bullets: Host cites a headline this week: after **AI-driven layoffs**, AI costs now exceed the labor savings.
Both agree the keywords are speed to market and productivity, not cost.
Lusk's joke: before AI, three unfinished projects; now 12 — people take on many more problems, which is what preserves jobs.

quote.text: Before AI I had three unfinished product projects and I've got 12.

themes.watch: The layoff-cost headline is cited from memory, with no source named.

takeaways.title: Make 'AI first, but you own the output' an explicit team rule.
Reposition engineers as the QA-and-production layer for AI-built tools rather than the builders of everything.
Measure AI ROI in time to market and projects shipped, not headcount saved.

hot_takes.take: The speed bump is actually the engineers, you know, that aren't adopting it because it completely displaces their identity as an engineer.
The cost of AI was actually more than the cost of the labor.

other_news.title: Sources referenced: Lane Castleman (Blockchain.com, a previous guest), builders sharing code on X, and an unnamed headline on AI layoffs costing more than they saved.

glossary.def: Attempting every task with AI before doing it manually, while staying responsible for the result.
How quickly a product goes from idea to customers.
